clue.text: The agent whose bride is bedecked

definitions.text: The agent whose bride is bedecked

parts.words: The agent whose bride is bedecked
parts.note: the bride is a vessel, which is 'bedecked' because it has decks; her husband is the shore agent who manages her affairs

explanation.surface: A man whose bride is decked out in her wedding finery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bedecked' looks like wedding finery, but it means fitted with decks: the bride is a vessel, traditionally 'she'.
explanation.definitionFit: This title names the owner's agent who sees to a vessel's repairs, stores and business in port.

clue.text: "Dwell I but in the — Of your good pleasure?" (J. Caesar)

definitions.text: "Dwell I but in the — Of your good pleasure?" (J. Caesar)

parts.words: "Dwell I but in the — Of your good pleasure?" (J. Caesar)
parts.note: Portia's line to Brutus asks if she lives only on the outskirts of his affection

explanation.surface: A quotation from Julius Caesar with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Portia, Brutus's wife, complains that she is kept on the edges of his life.
explanation.definitionFit: Portia uses the word for outlying districts of a town, meaning the fringes of his favour.

clue.text: I get less disorganized situated in water

indicators.note: disorganized means the letters of less are thrown out of order

explanation.surface: Someone becomes less chaotic when living by the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I get less' reads as a sentence about calming down; 'disorganized' is the anagram signal, and the definition describes islands rather than a person living by water.
explanation.definitionFit: Islands are pieces of land surrounded by sea.

clue.text: Dekker gave him a holiday

parts.note: Thomas Dekker's comedy is titled after a craftsman's holiday

explanation.surface: An employer named Dekker gives a worker time off.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Dekker's 1599 play is 'The Shoemaker's Holiday', about a cobbler who becomes Lord Mayor.
explanation.definitionFit: Dekker's Elizabethan comedy is titled after a cobbler's holiday.

clue.text: Hesitate, man, to make you a boss

parts.note: um is the sound of someone hesitating
bo is American slang for a man or pal

explanation.surface: A hesitant man is told to make someone the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' is not an employer but the raised knob at the centre of a shield.
explanation.definitionFit: The central knob on a shield, or a rounded protuberance, is a raised stud.

clue.text: For clothes for squares ?

parts.note: squares read as cubes or containers, so the fabric for dressing them takes their name

explanation.surface: Asking what fashionable gear is sold to old-fashioned people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Squares' looks like dull people; read it as boxes, and the fabric for them is a heavy woollen material used for coats.
explanation.definitionFit: A thick, felted woollen fabric used for riding coats and overcoats.

clue.text: Frosty old serving wench

definitions.meaning: the name given to waitresses in Lyons tea shops in the past

explanation.surface: A cold, unfriendly waitress of former times.
explanation.walkthrough: Lyons Corner Houses were a chain of British tea shops whose waitresses had this nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means chilly; the noun was the nickname of Lyons tea-shop waitresses.

clue.text: Still waters imprisoning bad air are pointedly dangerous

indicators.note: imprisoning means the still waters hold the next piece within them

parts.note: ponds are bodies of still water

indicators.note: bad means the letters of air are spoiled into a new order

explanation.surface: Stagnant ponds trap foul air and so are dangerous.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is descriptive: these daggers are dangerous at the point, hence 'pointedly'. 'Still waters' suggests the proverb, but simply means ponds.
explanation.definitionFit: Daggers are slender stabbing weapons, perilous because of their sharp tips.

clue.text: In Greece he will, as you see

parts.note: he will contracts to he'll

explanation.surface: In Greece a man will act as you can see.
explanation.walkthrough: HE'LL (he will) plus AS gives the Greeks' own name for their country.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek name for their homeland, used in English poetically.

clue.text: Where a dance turned to fisticuffs? X v. X?

parts.note: a ball is a formal dance

indicators.note: turned means the little word 'to' is flipped round

parts.note: to box is to fight with the fists

explanation.surface: A dance that ended in a punch-up, a rival against a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' flips TO to OT. X v. X is crosses against crosses: votes marked by rival voters.
explanation.definitionFit: Each X is a voter's cross, and the container where competing crosses are collected is the receptacle for votes.

clue.text: Your piano part, man, in 1984

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
a role is an actor's part

explanation.surface: Someone is given the piano part in a performance of a piece called 1984.
explanation.walkthrough: In Orwell's novel Nineteen Eighty-Four the working masses are called by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Orwell's novel the ordinary working people are known by this term, short for proletarian.

clue.text: Start again with the abstract ?

definitions.meaning: to carry on after a pause
a summary, as in a précis of a document

explanation.surface: A question about beginning again with a summary.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means continue after interruption; with an accent it is a summary or précis.

clue.text: Going to act Shakespeare, does it say?

definitions.text: Going to act Shakespeare, does it say?

parts.note: to play is to act on stage
Bill is the familiar form of William, Shakespeare's first name

explanation.surface: A question whether a notice announces a forthcoming performance of Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre poster announces which drama is going to be performed.

clue.text: Con men in the swim

parts.note: swindlers are given the name of predatory fish, and fish are in the swim

explanation.surface: Fraudsters who are fashionably in with the right crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the swim' means up to date socially, but here it puts the swindlers literally in the sea as predatory fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Swindlers are called by the name of these predatory fish, which also swim.

clue.text: Dyed water ? Try needling a copper for it !

definitions.text: Dyed water ? Try needling a copper for it !

parts.words: Dyed water ? Try needling a copper for it !
parts.note: Latin water plus a dye shade, and an engraving made by working a copper plate with a needle and acid

explanation.surface: Advice to annoy a policeman to get some coloured water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal plate used for this etching process, which uses acid (the 'water').
explanation.definitionFit: An etching process in which acid bites a copper plate to give tonal effects like wash drawings.

clue.text: They don't talk shop aboard ship

definitions.text: They don't talk shop aboard ship

parts.words: They don't talk shop aboard ship
parts.note: people who don't discuss work at sea, read instead as attendants who serve passengers rather than run a store

explanation.surface: Sailors who never discuss work while at sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Attendants on a liner serve passengers' meals and cabins rather than selling goods.

clue.text: Home guard against beastly penury ?

parts.note: keeping the wolf from the door means staving off poverty, so a hunting dog bred for wolves guards the house

explanation.surface: Asking about a defence force protecting homes from dreadful poverty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home guard' suggests Britain's wartime volunteer defence force; 'the wolf at the door' is an idiom for poverty, and this large dog was bred to hunt wolves.
explanation.definitionFit: A large hunting dog originally bred to kill the beasts that stand for poverty in the idiom.

clue.text: The principal's office

parts.note: not a room but the post held by the head of a school

explanation.surface: The room where the head teacher works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Office' looks like a room, but it means a post or position.
explanation.definitionFit: The position or tenure of a head teacher or chief.

clue.text: Fairies' coachmaker could provide R.L.S. with 24 sheets

indicators.note: could provide means the letters given can be rearranged to supply the answer

parts.note: a quire is a measure of paper, twenty-four sheets

explanation.surface: A suggestion that a fairy craftsman could supply Stevenson with paper.
explanation.walkthrough: In Romeo and Juliet Queen Mab's chariot is made by 'the joiner squirrel ... the fairies' coachmakers'. R.L.S. is Robert Louis Stevenson; 'could provide' rearranges RLS with QUIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mercutio's speech in Romeo and Juliet names this rodent as the joiner who builds Queen Mab's chariot.

clue.text: Tommy, I am out to join up

indicators.note: out means the letter for I is taken away from the soldier

parts.note: Tommy Atkins is the traditional name for a British private soldier

explanation.surface: A British soldier says he is leaving to enlist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'join up' looks like enlisting, but means fuse metal parts together.
explanation.definitionFit: To fuse metals together with a low-melting alloy is to unite them.

clue.text: Most exclusive, this shop

parts.note: a workplace where only union members are employed is the most exclusive kind of shop

explanation.surface: A boutique described as the most exclusive in town.
explanation.walkthrough: A closed shop is a workplace that only hires members of one trade union, so it shuts everyone else out.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop shut to non-union labour is the trade-union term for an exclusive workplace.

clue.text: The rude can be uncommonly vile

definitions.text: The rude can be uncommonly vile

indicators.note: uncommonly means the letters of rude can are set out in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Rough people can be unusually nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: The word survives mostly in the phrase 'durance vile', harsh imprisonment, and a 'rude can' is a rough jail.
explanation.definitionFit: The old word for imprisonment, usually followed by vile, fits a rough prison.

clue.text: Angular distance between bigot and freethinker ?

definitions.meaning: distance north or south of the equator measured in degrees
the freedom of opinion that separates an intolerant person from a liberal one

explanation.surface: The gap that separates a narrow-minded person from an open-minded one.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a geographical coordinate in degrees and freedom or tolerance of thought.

clue.text: Feeding lines in opposition

parts.note: the upper and lower rows in the mouth face one another and are used when eating

explanation.surface: Supply lines held by opposing forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeding lines' sounds military; read it as the rows in the jaw that oppose each other as you chew.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper and lower rows of biting structures in the mouth face each other.

clue.text: Hunting man's tot ?

definitions.meaning: a hunter is one who pursues game
a small drink of spirits, or the drink that follows one

explanation.surface: The little drink a huntsman takes.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's 's joins the two senses: one who pursues, and a drink that follows another.
explanation.definitionFit: A pursuer is one sense; the other is a small drink taken after another one.

clue.text: Even non-farmers may have a nodding acquaintance with these

definitions.text: Even non-farmers may have a nodding acquaintance with these

parts.words: Even non-farmers may have a nodding acquaintance with these
parts.note: insomniacs count these farm animals when nodding off to sleep

explanation.surface: People with no farming background still know a little about livestock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nodding acquaintance' means slight familiarity; here it is nodding off while counting animals jumping a fence.
explanation.definitionFit: Counting woolly farm animals is the traditional remedy for sleeplessness.

clue.text: Weird thing to do

parts.note: weird is the Scots noun for fate, and the Scots phrase for enduring it uses this verb

explanation.surface: Describing an odd action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weird' is not strange but the noun for fate: in Scots you 'dree your weird', endure your destiny.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scots verb meaning endure, used in the phrase about suffering one's fate.

clue.text: Lady Luck's old man

parts.note: old man is slang for husband; the partner of Lady Luck is the machine that picks Premium Bond winners

explanation.surface: Wondering who Lady Luck's husband might be.
explanation.walkthrough: ERNIE (Electronic Random Number Indicator Equipment) is the British machine that draws Premium Bond prizes.
explanation.definitionFit: The British computer that randomly picks Premium Bond prize winners has a man's name, fit as fortune's spouse.

clue.text: Such a task was for a temporary stableman

definitions.text: Such a task was for a temporary stableman

parts.words: Such a task was for a temporary stableman
parts.note: the hero who cleaned the Augean stables in a day was a stable hand only briefly

explanation.surface: A heavy job given to a casual stable worker.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the labours of Hercules was cleaning King Augeas's stables, so he was a stableman for one day.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge, laborious task is named after the Greek hero of twelve labours, one of them mucking out stables.

clue.text: For the farm worker something more than a crust

definitions.text: For the farm worker something more than a crust

parts.words: For the farm worker something more than a crust
parts.note: a meal belonging to a flock-tending farm hand, topped with mashed potato rather than pastry

explanation.surface: A farm labourer deserves more to eat than a crust of bread.
explanation.definitionFit: This dish of minced meat under mashed potato is named after a herdsman and has a topping instead of a pastry crust.
